next: Wednesday ~5:30 AM, or sooner if the forecast changes a lot
headline: Cold front Wednesday morning: heaviest rain likely 6–10 AM, close to a surge-boosted high tide. Models backed off on peak intensity this afternoon.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: A deepening low off the Pacific Northwest drags a strong cold front through the Bay Area Wednesday morning. NWS San Francisco expects rain to pick up 4–8 AM in the North Bay and sweep across the Peninsula roughly 6–10 AM, with isolated thunderstorms possible along the front. Showers and a better chance of thunderstorms follow Wednesday night into Thursday morning as colder air and a surface low move in. NWS storm totals through Friday morning: 1.5–2.5 in for most of the Bay Area. Another, weaker front arrives Saturday.

sections.title: Model trends
sections.text: The models agree on a soaking (about 2.5–2.9 in through Thursday as of this afternoon) but not on how hard the main burst hits. Around midday HRRR showed close to 0.9 in in a single hour around 7–8 AM and about 1.4 in for the wettest 3 hours, which would have been at or above the Mar 2023 and Dec 2022 floods. Later runs cut that back sharply, and RRFS, the NWS blend (NBM) and ECMWF were already lower (roughly 1.1, 1.0 and 0.8 in for the wettest 3 hours at their last check). I couldn't pull the very latest runs while writing this, because the forecast service wasn't responding, so the dashboard's live chart is the place for current numbers. A big drop between runs is common with frontal bands like this one; it doesn't mean the threat is over.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text: Redwood City high tide is predicted at 7.0 ft (MLLW) at 7:21 AM Wednesday, and NOAA's Bay model adds about 1.5 ft of surge (near 8.6 ft). NWS has a Coastal Flood Advisory from 5 AM Wednesday to 10 AM Thursday. The Bay can't reach the street directly, but a high Bay keeps the Bayfront Canal and Atherton Channel from draining, so the channel can't take water as fast while the heaviest rain may be falling. That overlap is the setup to watch. Thursday's high is a bit higher (7.4 ft predicted at 7:58 AM), in case the Thursday-morning thunderstorms deliver a second burst.

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Dry this afternoon. Atherton Channel at Caltrain is essentially empty (0.07 ft; the sensor reads dry below about 0.4 ft), so the system starts with all of its capacity. The ground is damp from Sunday and Monday's rain, so runoff will come quickly.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Three things could make Wednesday worse than the latest numbers suggest. (1) Frontal rain bands are narrow: a 10–20 mile shift decides whether the heaviest core passes over Atherton. (2) HRRR has under-forecast every big local burst in our records, by about 3× in the worst cases (Mar 2023, Dec 2025). (3) Any thunderstorm along the front can drop 0.5 in in 20–30 minutes. Timing is uncertain by about ±2 hours, which decides how much it overlaps with the high tide. Most likely outcome: water to the garage doors (Yellow) at the peak. Garage + (Red) is plausible if the burst reaches about 1.2 in in 3 hours. Structure-level flooding (Purple) needs a much bigger burst than current guidance shows.

sections.title: What to do tonight
sections.text:
• Move cars out of the cul-de-sac before 6 AM.
• Clear leaves from the street drain grates, yard drains and the ditch behind the houses this evening. The first big wind of the season brings down leaves, and a clogged grate floods the street at much lower rain totals.
• Seal the dryer vent and low wall openings, and set sandbags at the garage door and the back of the house.
• Wind Advisory overnight with gusts up to 50 mph near the coast: power outages are possible. The pump station needs power. If you lose power during the burst, assume the pumps may be slow and watch the street closely. Whether the station has backup power is a question for the county.
• Glance at the pump station's status lights tonight if it's easy to; a red light before the storm is worth reporting.
• During the peak, take a photo of the street with the time visible. Every documented storm improves the warning levels.
• Keep the dashboard open in a tab. It records the forecast vs. what actually falls, which improves the bias factor, and the 1-hour burst alarm needs live readings.
• Don't drive or walk through moving water on the street.
